q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS TOTAL FROM PRODUCT)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER C GROUP BY CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(*) AS TOTAL FROM PRODUCT)
counterexample: INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2), (3); INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 1), (2, 2);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent because Q1 uses COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) in the HAVING clause, while Q2 uses COUNT(*) AS TOTAL. COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) in Q1 considers the unique product keys associated with each customer, whereas COUNT(*) AS TOTAL in Q2 considers the total number of products in the PRODUCT table.
counterexample_dsp: The difference is triggered when a customer has the same product key as another customer, but the total number of products in the PRODUCT table is different from the number of unique product keys associated with the customers.
